content: Epazote, also known as Wormseed, Jesuit's Tea, Mexican Tea, or Herba Sancti Mariæ (scientific name: Chenopodium ambrosioides), is a herbaceous plant native to regions of Central America, South America, and southern Mexico. It is an annual or short-lived perennial plant that can grow to a height of 1 to 2 meters. The plant has an irregular branching pattern and features oblong-lanceolate leaves that can reach up to 12 centimeters in length. Its flowers are small, green, and grow in a branched panicle located at the apex of the stem. While epazote is indigenous to its native regions, it is also cultivated in warm temperate and subtropical areas, including parts of Europe and the United States, such as Missouri, New England, and the Eastern United States. In some cases, it has become an invasive weed. The term epazote is derived from the Nahuatl word epazōtl, which entered the Spanish language. Culinary Uses Epazote is utilized both as a leaf vegetable and as a culinary herb, primarily for its distinctive and pungent flavor. When consumed raw, it has a resinous and medicinal taste, which has been likened to the licorice-like flavors of anise, fennel, or tarragon, but with a much stronger intensity. Its aroma is potent and challenging to describe, with comparisons ranging from citrus and petroleum to savory, mint, and even putty. Traditionally, epazote is used in Mexican cuisine, particularly in dishes involving black beans, where it is valued not only for its flavor but also for its reputed antiflatulent properties. Beyond beans, it is employed to season a variety of traditional Mexican dishes, including quesadillas and sopes (especially those containing huitlacoche), soups, mole de olla, tamales with cheese and chile, chilaquiles, eggs, potatoes, and enchiladas. Medicinal Uses Epazote has a long history of medicinal applications, in addition to its culinary uses. It is traditionally believed to alleviate flatulence caused by the consumption of beans. Furthermore, it has been used in the treatment of various conditions, including amenorrhea (absence of menstruation), dysmenorrhea (painful menstruation), malaria, chorea (a movement disorder), hysteria, catarrh (inflammation of mucous membranes), and asthma. The plant is also the source of oil of chenopodium, which has anthelmintic properties, meaning it is capable of killing intestinal worms. Historically, this oil was listed in the United States Pharmacopoeia for its medicinal use. Additionally, epazote has been cited as an antispasmodic and abortifacient. Notably, early research on epazote contributed to the development of the first birth control pills. The essential oil of epazote contains a high concentration of ascaridole, which can make up as much as 70% of its composition. Other components of the oil include limonene, p-cymene, and smaller amounts of various monoterpenes and their derivatives, such as α-pinene, myrcene, terpinene, thymol, camphor, and trans-isocarveol. Ascaridole, chemically known as 1,4-peroxido-p-menth-2-ene, is an uncommon compound in spices. Another plant that owes much of its character to this monoterpene peroxide is boldo. Ascaridole is toxic and has a strong, unpleasant flavor. In its pure form, it is highly explosive and sensitive to shock. Interestingly, the ascaridole content in epazote is reportedly lower in plants grown in Mexico compared to those cultivated in Europe or Asia.
